Formerly the Duke of Zhou carried King Cheng on his back, making this robe; down to today it is taken as court dress.
Formerly the Duke of Zhou carried King Cheng on his back and made this item of dress; down to the present it is used as court dress.

周公負成王 identifies the Duke of Zhou as carrying King Cheng on his back, and 制此服衣 reports making this item of dress. The conjunction preserves those clauses without requiring the carrying and making to have been simultaneous or specifying an entire robe; 至今以為朝服 reports its continued use as court dress.
Myth credits the Zhou regent’s baby-carrying sash for today’s court pouch.
Long ago, the Duke of Zhou carried King Cheng on his back and made this item of dress, which is still used as court dress today.

The source explicitly names the Duke of Zhou and King Cheng and reports carrying and making, then continued use as court dress. It does not state Cheng's age, describe a baby-carrying sash, or classify this account as myth. The following unit offers an uncertain alternate account, so this translation does not assert historical verification of the reported origin.
